justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with only modest drift over time. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 231.5 is anchored heavily on recent price action and momentum, assuming no major overnight catalysts materialize. The slight upward drift to 232.0 at one week and 233.0 at one month reflects a mild positive bias consistent with longer-run trend expectations, but the incremental increases are small because I did not want to overweight directional conviction when the near-term environment appeared relatively range-bound. Essentially, I was treating the current level as a reasonable equilibrium with only gentle mean-drift assumptions layered on top.

The confidence interval widths expand significantly as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the standard accumulation of uncertainty over time. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly plus or minus 8.5 points captures typical intraday-to-next-day volatility, including normal gap risk and intraday swings. By one week, the interval widens to plus or minus 16 points, accounting for the possibility of several volatile sessions compounding. At one month, the interval stretches to plus or minus 30 points, reflecting the reality that over four to five weeks, macro data surprises, earnings releases, Federal Reserve communications, and geopolitical developments can all shift sentiment meaningfully. The asymmetry in the monthly interval is relatively modest, suggesting I did not assign dramatically different probabilities to large upside versus large downside scenarios at the time.

Several specific risks could push outcomes well outside my stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a sharp jobs miss, a credit event, or escalating geopolitical conflict — could produce a move well below the lower bound of the monthly interval. On the upside, a surprisingly dovish policy signal from the Federal Reserve or a resolution of trade or geopolitical tensions could fuel a rally beyond the upper bound. Liquidity conditions and market positioning also matter; if the market is crowded in one direction, an unwind could amplify moves beyond what fundamentals alone would suggest.

Finally, it is worth noting that interval estimates at longer horizons carry an inherent epistemological limitation: tail events that are genuinely hard to anticipate — such as sudden financial contagion, a major geopolitical shock, or a policy error — are by definition underweighted in any historically calibrated volatility model. My stated 90% intervals should be understood as reflecting normal to moderately stressed conditions, not worst-case scenarios. Users should treat the monthly interval especially as a central tendency guide rather than a hard boundary on plausible outcomes.
